section.title: Oppression and Companionship
section.sectionRationale: The Teacher turns from the sweep of the seasons to the raw underside of life under the sun: the tears of the oppressed with no comforter, the restless envy that drives all our striving, and the loneliness that makes wealth taste of nothing. Against that ache he sets one of the warmest notes in the book, two are better than one, before exposing even popularity and power as vapor. The chapter diagnoses the pains that money and success cannot cure and points quietly toward the gifts of companionship and, beyond them, to God.
section.thesis: Under the sun oppression goes uncomforted, striving is fueled by envy, and both loneliness and applause prove to be vapor; yet companionship is a real good, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken, hinting that we were made for one another and for the God who is the true Comforter.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the tears of the oppressed with no comforter; the envy that drives our toil and the lonely miser it produces; the good of companionship, two are better than one; and the fleeting favor of the crowd, where even a wise young king is soon forgotten.

verses.text: Again I looked, and I considered all the oppression taking place under the sun. I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter; the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter.
So I admired the dead, who had already died, above the living, who are still alive.
But better than both is he who has not yet existed, who has not seen the evil that is done under the sun.
I saw that all labor and success spring from a man’s envy of his neighbor. This too is {{hevel|futile}} and a pursuit of the wind.
The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.
Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind.
Again, I saw {{hevel|futility}} under the sun.

There is a man all alone, without even a son or brother. And though there is no end to his labor, his eyes are still not content with his wealth: “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” This too is {{hevel|futile}}, a miserable task.
Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.
For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up!
Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?
And though one may be overpowered, two can resist. Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken.

units.label: The fleeting favor of the crowd
units.note: even the king is soon forgotten

verses.text: Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.
For the youth has come from the prison to the kingship, though he was born poor in his own kingdom.
I saw that all who lived and walked under the sun followed this second one, the youth who succeeded the king.
There is no limit to all the people who were before them. Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later. This too is {{hevel|futile}} and a pursuit of the wind.

hevel.gloss: Vapor, breath, mist. The keyword of Ecclesiastes, rendered futile, futility, or meaningless. It names how life under the sun slips through the fingers like breath on a cold day. Here it lands on envy driven striving, on the lonely miser's endless toil, and on the crowd's short lived applause, all of which vanish like vapor.

basic.context: The Teacher looks at the hard realities that wealth and success cannot fix. First he sees the tears of the oppressed who have no one to comfort them, and the sight is so bitter he almost envies the dead. Then he names the engine under most of our hard work: envy, wanting to outdo the neighbor, which turns out to be chasing the wind. He tells of a lonely man who piles up money with no one to share it and finally asks, for whom am I doing this? Against all this he sets a warm truth: two are better than one, and a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. Finally he shows that even a popular young ruler is soon forgotten. Money, striving, and applause cannot fill the ache; companionship is a real gift, and the deeper answer lies with God.
basic.hermeneutics: The Teacher is not endorsing withdrawal from life or telling us to give up. He is diagnosing the pain beneath oppression, rivalry, and loneliness so honestly that we stop expecting our striving to satisfy us. The repeated comforter in verse 1 aches with an absence, and the whole chapter presses toward the gifts God gives: companions who lift us up, and ultimately the God who is the true Comforter. The praise of companionship in verses 9 to 12 is genuine wisdom for how to live, not merely another example of vapor.
basic.originalLanguages: One word ties the chapter together: hevel, vapor or breath, the book's name for what is fleeting. It falls on the envy that drives our labor, verse 4, on the lonely toiler's endless striving, verses 7 and 8, and on the crowd's applause that fades within a generation, verse 16. Each thing looks solid and turns out to be as thin as breath, which is why the Teacher keeps steering us away from them and toward what God actually gives.
basic.typology: The cry of the oppressed who have no comforter looks ahead to the Comforter God sends, the Spirit whom Christ promised, and to Christ Himself who binds up the brokenhearted. The good of two together, the friend who lifts the fallen, points to the fellowship of the people of God and to Christ the friend who came to seek and save. The cord of three strands has long been read as a picture of a bond that God Himself strengthens.
basic.christ: Into a world of tears with no comforter, God sends His Son to proclaim comfort to all who mourn, and then sends the Spirit, the Comforter, to dwell with His people forever. The lonely miser's question, for whom do I toil, is answered in Christ, who redeems our labor and gathers us into a family. Jesus is the friend closer than a brother, the one who lifts the fallen, so that the ache the Teacher exposes finds its rest in Him.
basic.god: God is not indifferent to injustice; the Teacher's grief at the tears of the oppressed reflects God's own concern, and the book will insist that God judges every deed. God is the giver of companionship, weaving human beings together so they are not left alone. And He is the true Comforter whose absence the chapter feels so sharply, the one who finally answers the cry that no earthly power can.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 3 shows God seeing the affliction of His people and coming down to deliver. Isaiah 61 promises comfort to all who mourn. John 14 gives the Spirit as another Comforter. Proverbs 18 speaks of a friend who sticks closer than a brother.
basic.oneStory: Ecclesiastes 4 lays bare the pains that success cannot heal: injustice with no comforter, striving born of envy, and the loneliness of wealth held alone. It offers one steady light, the gift of companionship, and leaves the deeper ache pointing beyond the sun. The canon answers it in the God who sees the oppressed, sends His Son as the friend of sinners, and pours out the Spirit as the Comforter the Teacher longed for.

context.literary:
The chapter is a chain of five short observations, each opened by a verb of looking: 'again I looked,' verse 1; 'I saw,' verse 4; 'again, I saw,' verse 7; and the closing instance in verses 13 to 16. Between them sit proverbs, which the Teacher uses as quick strokes of commentary. The effect is of a man walking through the marketplace of life with his eyes open and reporting what he sees.

The most striking device is a play on numbers. Verse 8 describes a man who is 'one,' without a second: the Hebrew sets 'one' against 'second' in a bare phrase. Verses 9 to 12 then go through 'two' and 'three,' and verses 13 to 16 come back to 'the second' youth who succeeds the king. Alone, two, three, second: the chapter is built on counting, and each number is a different answer to the same loneliness. The famous proverb on the three-fold cord is the climax of this arithmetic, as an ascending series, one, two, three, which is a pattern of rising numbers also found in Proverbs 30.

The proverbs are arranged with care. Verse 4 diagnoses the root of ambition as envy, verse 5 names the opposite fault, laziness, and verse 6 offers a middle way: a handful with rest. A reader who stopped at verse 4 would conclude that all work is poisoned, and one who stopped at verse 5 would conclude that idleness is wise. The Teacher refuses both.

The chapter's first panel, verses 1 to 3, is the darkest in the book so far, and its logic runs downhill: the oppressed, then the dead who are better off, then the unborn who are better still. The last panel, verses 13 to 16, ends in the same refrain that closed the previous chapters, and its irony is that even the popular rise of a poor young king is forgotten by those who come after. The chapter therefore opens in tears and ends in forgotten applause.
context.historical:
The Teacher looks at a society where power sat at the top and the weak had few ways to be heard. Verse 1 is the cry of people under officials, landlords and creditors. The Law had already set up protections: do not oppress a poor hired hand, Deuteronomy 24:14; do not mistreat the widow or orphan, Exodus 22:22-24. The prophets complain again and again that those protections were ignored, as in Amos 5:12 and Micah 2:1-2. Ecclesiastes 5:8 adds that a province's officials are watched by officials above them, and so oppression is rarely a single villain's work but a chain of interests.

The remark that labor and success spring from envy of one's neighbor, verse 4, fits a culture where honor and standing were measured against others in the village and the clan. The Tenth Commandment guarded against that covetousness, Exodus 20:17, and the wisdom tradition warned that 'envy rots the bones,' Proverbs 14:30.

The praise of companionship in verses 9 to 12 has everyday settings. Travelers on the roads were exposed to robbers and wild beasts, so journeys were made in company. A fallen traveler needed someone to help him up. In the cold nights of the hill country, sleeping together for warmth was ordinary. The 'cord of three strands' also reflects a craft: a rope twisted from three strands is far stronger than any one of them.

The closing story of the poor wise youth and the old foolish king, verses 13 to 16, is a parable that fits many known careers. In Israel's history Joseph moved from a dungeon to second place beside Pharaoh, Genesis 41:14, 41:40. Jehoiachin was lifted from prison to a seat above other kings, 2 Kings 25:27-30. Jeroboam, a servant of Solomon, was told that he would rule, 1 Kings 11:26-40. The Teacher names none of them. He draws a pattern that readers in many courts would recognize: the crowd follows the new young ruler, and a generation later the crowd is gone.
context.canonical:
The chapter opens with a Hebrew word that the rest of the Bible treats as sacred: 'comforter.' Isaiah 40:1 begins the great consolation of Israel with 'Comfort, comfort My people.' The Teacher notes twice that the oppressed had none. In Exodus 3:7, by contrast, the LORD says that He has seen the affliction of His people, heard their cry and is aware of their sufferings. Psalm 12:5 and Psalm 10:14 say that God sees trouble and grief and will arise for the groaning of the needy. Proverbs 14:31 says that oppressing the poor taunts their Maker. The Teacher's complaint is therefore not that the Bible's God does not care, but that on the visible surface of life nobody, including the powerful, plays the comforter.

Verses 9 to 12 pick up Genesis 2:18: 'It is not good for the man to be alone.' Proverbs 27:17 speaks of iron sharpening iron, and Proverbs 18:24 of a friend who sticks closer than a brother. In the New Testament the same logic becomes the life of the church: 'Carry one another's burdens,' Galatians 6:2, 'encourage and build one another up,' 1 Thessalonians 5:11, and 'let us not neglect meeting together,' Hebrews 10:24-25. Jesus sent His disciples out two by two, Mark 6:7, and Luke 10:1, and said that where two or three gather in His name He is among them, Matthew 18:20.

The envy of verse 4 is condemned again in James 3:16, where jealousy and selfish ambition lead to every evil practice. The folly of verse 5 meets the sluggard of Proverbs 6:6-11 and 24:33-34, and the better-than proverb of verse 6 has a close sister in Proverbs 15:16-17. The tears of the oppressed reach heaven in James 5:4: 'The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher wants his hearers to look at injustice without turning away and without pretending to fix it. The first verses are a refusal to be glib. He does not tell the oppressed to be thankful, and he does not argue that their pain serves a purpose. He only says what he sees, and that no one is there to comfort them. A people who had to be reminded that the poor existed among them needed that honesty.

He wants them next to see themselves in the engine of their own ambition. Behind a great deal of hard work and apparent achievement is envy, a measuring of oneself against the neighbor. The hearers are meant to ask why they work and whom they are trying to beat.

He wants them to value people over profit. The miser of verse 8 is unforgettable: he has no heir, no friend, no end to his work, and no answer to his own question, 'for whom do I toil?' The Teacher puts that question in the miser's mouth so that his hearers will ask it of themselves. His answer is companionship, a rope of several strands. And he closes with a warning against putting hope in popularity or in the rise of a promising leader, since the crowd moves on.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first three verses record the Teacher's reaction to oppression, and they are descriptive. His conclusion that the dead and the unborn are better off than the living is the low point of a man looking only at the earthly scene. It is not a recommendation. The book itself argues against it: 'even a live dog is better than a dead lion,' 9:4, and the call to enjoy life in 9:7-9. Believers who suffer should not read verses 2 and 3 as spiritual advice, but as an honest voice that stands in the same line as Job 3 and Jeremiah 20:14-18. Scripture lets the grieving speak, and then it answers.

The proverbs of verses 9 to 12 are different in force. They describe real goods and invite the reader to act on them: choose companions, help the fallen, build bonds that can bear weight. These are teachings with the force of wisdom, and the New Testament takes them up as commands for the church. A modern reader can apply them to marriage, friendship, the congregation and the small group.

Verses 13 to 16 are an observation of how popularity works. They do not tell leaders to be unpopular or people to avoid following wise leaders. They warn against measuring a life by applause.

debates.question: Is the Teacher advising despair when he says the dead and the unborn are better off, verses 2 and 3?

views.label: A sincere but partial verdict
views.case: These verses state where an observer lands if he looks only at oppression and has no one to bring comfort. They are a true report of one view from the ground, similar to Job 3:11-19 and Jeremiah 20:14-18, and they should be read as a cry, not as doctrine.

views.label: A rhetorical step the book later corrects
views.case: The book's own later words contradict the claim. Ecclesiastes 9:4 says a living dog is better than a dead lion, and 11:7 says that light is sweet. The extreme statement is placed early so that the reader can see how far an observer goes when he refuses to bring God into the picture.

views.label: A prophetic protest
views.case: Others hear the verses as a protest against injustice so heavy that the Teacher cannot call life good when so many suffer. On that reading the verdict is aimed at the oppressors more than at existence, and it presses the reader to care about the oppressed.

debates.bearing: The first and second views fit the text best. The verses are honest but not final, and the Bible's answer to the tears of the oppressed is a God who sees and a Savior who comforts, not a verdict that nonexistence is best.

debates.question: Who are the poor youth and the old king in verses 13 to 16?

views.label: A specific historical pair
views.case: Interpreters have proposed Joseph and Pharaoh, David and Saul, Jeroboam and Rehoboam, or others from the ancient Near East, because each fits parts of the story: a youth who came out of confinement or poverty and rose to power. No one fits every detail.

views.label: A general pattern
views.case: The text names no one and speaks in the language of a proverbial tale. The Teacher may be offering a type of story that repeats in every age, with the point that popularity is short-lived whichever names are filled in.

views.label: A reference to a figure in the Teacher's own day
views.case: A few take the verses as a pointed reference to someone the first hearers knew, which would explain the detail but leaves us unable to identify him.

debates.bearing: The point of the passage does not hang on the identification. Whoever the characters were, the Teacher draws the same lesson: the crowd that followed the youth does not remember him, and a wise reader should not look to political fortunes for lasting joy.

debates.question: Is envy the true source of all work, verse 4?

views.label: A sweeping claim about motives
views.case: The verse says that all labor and success spring from envy. Read literally, it makes rivalry the engine of every project and every skill.

views.label: A realistic exaggeration
views.case: Wisdom literature uses broad statements to make a point. The claim is that envy contaminates far more of our work than we admit, not that no work is done from love, which the book allows in other places.

debates.bearing: Either way the verse invites an examination of motives, and Proverbs 14:30 and James 3:16 confirm that envy is a real and serious enemy.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the chapter's burden is ashuqim, 'oppressions,' from the root ashaq, to press down or exploit. It is used for the treatment of a hired hand in Deuteronomy 24:14, where the LORD forbids oppressing a poor and needy worker. The Teacher saw the thing the Law was written to prevent.

The word 'comforter,' menachem, is repeated in the same verse, and it comes from nacham, the verb of Isaiah 40:1, 'Comfort, comfort My people.' The repetition is the Teacher's own refrain of grief. In John 14:16 Jesus promises 'another Advocate,' the Greek paraklētos, a word of the same family of ideas, the one called alongside to help. The word 'another' suggests that Jesus has been the first. The Teacher's cry that the oppressed had no comforter is met by that promise.

In verse 2 the Teacher says he 'admired' the dead, from the verb shabach, to praise or commend. The same verb returns in 8:15, 'I commended the enjoyment of life.' The book is full of his commendations, and it is instructive that the same verb is used for his low-point praise of the dead and his later praise of joy.

The 'envy' of verse 4, qin'ah, is the word translated 'jealousy' or 'zeal' elsewhere; its flavor depends on context. The Greek zēlos in James 3:16 is the New Testament counterpart, joined there with selfish ambition. 'Success' in the BSB renders a rare word for skill or achievement. The verse says that skill itself is driven by rivalry.

Verse 5 says the fool 'folds his hands,' chovek yadav, a posture of idleness also found in Proverbs 6:10 and 24:33. The verb is the same one that appears in 3:5 for embracing. The fool hugs himself instead of working. He 'consumes his own flesh,' a vivid image of self-destruction by sloth.

The proverb of verse 6 sets two measures against each other. The 'handful' is kaph, the palm of one hand. The 'two handfuls' is chofnayim, both hands cupped. The Teacher says one palm of rest is better than two full hands of toil. 'Tranquility,' nachat, is quiet rest.

Verse 8 is built on a compact phrase: yesh echad ve-ein sheni, 'there is one, and no second.' The phrase is plain Hebrew arithmetic and gives the chapter its counting theme. It also echoes Genesis 2:18, where the first thing in creation called 'not good' is the man's being alone. Verse 9 opens with shenayim, 'two,' and the 'good return' is sachar, the ordinary word for wages or reward. Companions give a return in the same coin as labor.

In verse 10 the cry 'pity' is the rare ve-ilo, a cry of woe over the lone faller. In verse 12 the 'cord of three strands' is chut ha-meshullash, and the word for 'quickly' is bimherah. A threefold cord is not easily snapped.

Verse 13 says the old king no longer knows how to take a warning, from zahar, the verb used of a watchman who warns in Ezekiel 33:7. The king has stopped listening to his watchmen. The poor youth is a yeled, a word for a young person; the king is zaqen ukesil, 'old and foolish,' a contrast of age and wisdom that overturns the usual expectation that the old are wise.

typology.type: The oppressed with no comforter, Ecclesiastes 4:1
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher's picture of tears without a comforter finds its answer in a series of ways. God had told Moses He had seen the affliction of His people and heard their cry, Exodus 3:7, and Isaiah 40:1 begins with 'Comfort, comfort My people.' In Jesus these promises take a body. He reads Isaiah 61, 'to preach good news to the poor... to release the oppressed,' Luke 4:18, He weeps at a grave, John 11:35, and calls the weary to Himself, Matthew 11:28. He then promises another Advocate, John 14:16. The correspondence is that the very thing the Teacher misses, a comforter, is given. The type falls short of Christ in that the oppressed in Ecclesiastes simply wait, while the oppressed in the Gospels are met.

typology.type: The cord of three strands, Ecclesiastes 4:9-12
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher's proverb is about people, but Scripture lets it point beyond them. Genesis 2:18 shows God declaring aloneness not good, and Christ, the bridegroom, joins a people to Himself, Ephesians 5:25-32. He sends His disciples out in pairs, Luke 10:1, and promises to be present where two or three gather in His name, Matthew 18:20. The Teacher's cord holds because the strands are bound together; the church holds because of the One who binds. The type is incomplete because the proverb says nothing about a third who is God, though a Christian reader may hear that echo. It remains a proverb, not a doctrine of the Trinity, and the text does not require more.

typology.type: The poor youth who rises from prison, Ecclesiastes 4:13-16
typology.fulfillment: The parable of a poor wise youth who goes from confinement to kingship is a shadow of Joseph, who came from the dungeon to stand second only to Pharaoh, Genesis 41:14, 41:40, and a faint shadow of the Servant who became poor to make others rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. In Christ, humiliation to death on a cross is followed by God's exaltation to the highest place, Philippians 2:8-11. The crucial difference is the end of the story. The Teacher's youth is forgotten by those who come after, verse 16, while of Christ it is said, 'His kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:33, and 'His dominion is an everlasting dominion,' Daniel 7:14.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the sight of tears with no comforter. The Gospel of Luke records that Jesus announced His mission in the words of Isaiah, to bring good news to the poor and to release the oppressed, Luke 4:18, and Isaiah 53:3 describes Him as 'a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.' The Teacher had to say that the oppressed had no comforter. The Gospel can say that the Man of sorrows came to stand with them, and Hebrews 4:15 says that He sympathizes with our weaknesses. 2 Corinthians 1:3-4 calls the Father 'the God of all comfort,' who comforts us so that we can comfort others.

It leads to Christ by the loneliness of verses 8 to 12. The man alone, with no second, finds in the New Testament a Savior who does not leave His people alone. Jesus calls His followers friends, John 15:15, sends them out in pairs, and promises His presence where they gather. He also takes on Himself the loneliest hour in history: He cried out in forsakenness on the cross, Matthew 27:46, so that no one who trusts Him is forsaken. The Teacher says pity the one who falls with no one to lift him up. Christ is the One who stoops to the fallen.

It leads to Christ by the contrast in verses 13 to 16. The youth who rises from prison to kingship is celebrated and then forgotten. Christ is the poor One who became poor for our sakes, 2 Corinthians 8:9, died and rose, and was given the name above every name, Philippians 2:9-11. He is the king who is not forgotten, because He is not dead. The Teacher's warning that the next generation does not rejoice in its predecessor's rise is answered by Luke 1:33 and Daniel 7:14.

It leads to Christ by the unmasking of envy. The Teacher says labor springs from rivalry. Christ's work sprang from love, and He gave Himself for His enemies. Philippians 2:3-8 sets humility against selfish ambition and holds up Christ's emptying of Himself as the pattern. We should be careful not to read every detail of the chapter as a hidden Christ. The better path is to see that the needs the Teacher exposes, comfort for the oppressed, companionship for the lonely, a king who lasts, and a heart free from envy, are the needs the gospel meets.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who is hidden in the Teacher's survey but not absent from the world. The name of God does not appear in the chapter at all. That silence is the Teacher's method, and it makes the reader feel the weight of a world observed without the lights on. But the rest of Scripture says that God sees. In Psalm 10:14 the psalmist says to God, 'You have regarded trouble and grief,' and in Psalm 12:5 the LORD says He will arise for the cause of the oppressed. The tears of verse 1 are not unnoticed in heaven, and James 5:4 says the cries of the harvesters reach the ears of the Lord of Hosts.

The chapter shows God as the one who made people for each other. The proverbs of two and three are not mere good advice. They rest on the creation judgment that it is not good for the man to be alone, Genesis 2:18, and on the revealed character of a God who 'settles the lonely in families,' Psalm 68:6. A theology of God that leaves out friendship, marriage and the church is thinner than the Bible's.

The chapter also holds a quiet judgment on how we treat one another. Proverbs 14:31 says whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, and Proverbs 22:22-23 says that the LORD will take up their case. The oppressor in verse 1 is not only a public problem; he is in rebellion against the God who made the weak. And the envious person of verse 4 is in rebellion against God's provision, because envy denies that what the neighbor has was given.

God is also shown in what He is not. He is not the crowd that forgets, and He is not the fickle ruler whose praise fades. The chapter's last verse says the successor will not be celebrated by those who come later, and Psalm 146:3-4 explains why: do not trust princes, whose plans perish on the day their spirit leaves. The God who does not die is the only one whose glory does not run out.

For worship this means two things. We bring the cry of the oppressed into prayer, because God has said He hears it, Exodus 22:23. And we receive the company of other believers as His gift, not a luxury, for the Teacher shows how fragile we are when alone.

crossReferences.note: God tells Moses He has seen the affliction of His people, heard their cry because of their oppressors, and knows their sufferings. It is the divine answer to the Teacher's observation of tears with no comforter: heaven sees what the earth ignores.

The Law forbids oppressing a poor and needy hired hand, whether a fellow Israelite or a foreigner. The oppression the Teacher sees is exactly the sin the Law named, which shows he is not describing a natural fact but a moral failure.

A tranquil heart gives life to the body, but envy rots the bones. It supports the Teacher's diagnosis of verse 4 and offers the alternative that verse 6 commends, a heart at rest rather than a body driven by rivalry.

The ant works without an overseer, and the slacker's folded hands bring poverty like a robber. It fills in verse 5: the Teacher is not praising idleness but showing that the fool who folds his hands destroys himself.
The first thing God calls not good in creation is that the man is alone. Verses 8 to 12 are an application of that verdict to the daily realities of work, travel and cold nights.

Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. The Teacher's proverb speaks of help in need, and this one adds that a companion shapes and sharpens a person, so friendship is both rescue and growth.
Carrying one another's burdens fulfills the law of Christ. It lifts the picture of the fallen traveler and the companion who helps him up into the shape of Christian love.
Where two or three gather in Christ's name, He is with them. The number language of verses 9 to 12 is gathered into His promise of presence, which turns a cord of three into something stronger still.
Joseph is brought quickly from the dungeon to stand before Pharaoh and is made second only to the throne in verse 40. He is the closest biblical picture of the youth who goes from prison to kingship.
Do not trust princes, for when their spirit departs they return to the ground and their plans perish. It explains why the crowd's loyalty to the new king in verses 15 and 16 ends in forgetfulness.
Christ humbled Himself to death on a cross, and God exalted Him to the highest place. He is the rising king whose name is not forgotten but confessed by every tongue.
The cries of the harvesters whose wages were withheld have reached the Lord of Hosts. It answers verse 1 directly: the oppressed are heard, and their oppressors will answer for it.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 does not stop at the first sin. By Genesis 4 there is murder, and within a few chapters there is violence over the whole earth. Ecclesiastes 4 is a window into that world, where power lies on the side of the oppressor and the weak have no one. The passage answers the question of how a good creation came to hold so much pain, and its answer is the same as the rest of the Bible's: the human heart, with its envy and its greed, has made it so.

It also holds up what was lost. Man was made for company, Genesis 2:18, and for work that was good, and both are damaged. Envy turns work into contest, and aloneness turns wealth into emptiness. The passage sets up the need for a restoration of both, a community where burdens are carried and labor is no longer a rivalry.

God starts that restoration with a people. He hears Israel's cry in Egypt, Exodus 3:7, and gives laws that protect the poor, and His prophets keep naming oppression as the sin that most provokes Him. When His Son comes He announces good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, and builds a community of those who carry each other's burdens, Galatians 6:2. The church is meant to be a cord of many strands.

The Teacher's grief over the king who rises and is forgotten also prepares for a King who is not forgotten. Daniel 7:14 sees one given everlasting dominion, and Philippians 2:9-11 shows Him exalted. The pattern of earthly kings, who are celebrated and then forgotten, is broken by the one King who died and lives.

The story ends with the tears of verse 1 wiped away. Isaiah 25:8 promises that the Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face, and Revelation 21:4 shows God doing it, in a world with no more mourning or crying or pain. In that world no one is alone: 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. The oppressed finally have a Comforter, and the lonely have a home. Until then the church lives in the world of Ecclesiastes 4, looking at oppression with open eyes, choosing companions, resisting envy, and trusting the God who sees.

quiz.q: What grieves the Teacher most about the oppression he sees in 4:1?

options.text: That the oppressed had no comforter while power stayed with their oppressors.
options.note: The repeated no comforter is the aching center of the verse.

options.text: That there was so much oppression happening under the sun.
options.note: The scale grieves him, but the sharpest pain is the absence of any comforter.

options.text: That the oppressors were more powerful than the weak.
options.note: The power imbalance is noted, yet the emphasis falls on the lack of comfort.

options.text: That oppression could never be judged by anyone.
options.note: Elsewhere the book insists God will judge every deed; this verse laments the missing comforter.

quiz.q: According to 4:4, what drives much of our labor and success?

options.text: Envy of our neighbor, a striving that proves to be chasing the wind.
options.note: The Teacher names rivalry as the hidden engine, and calls it vapor.

options.text: A restless comparison with others that never satisfies.
options.note: A fair paraphrase, though the text specifically names envy of the neighbor.

options.text: A simple desire to provide for one's needs.
options.note: Honest provision is good; the verse targets envy driven striving.

options.text: The joy of work as a gift from God.
options.note: That is a different theme; here the driver exposed is envy, not gift.

quiz.q: What does the Teacher commend in 4:9-12?

options.text: Companionship, because two are better than one and a cord of three strands is not quickly broken.
options.note: The passage praises the real good of friends who help and strengthen one another.

options.text: The value of having people to help you when you fall.
options.note: True to verse 10, but the section widens to the whole good of companionship.

options.text: Working in teams so you can produce more wealth.
options.note: The point is mutual support and warmth, not maximizing output.

options.text: Staying alone so no one can take advantage of you.
options.note: This reverses the passage, which laments the one who is alone.

quiz.q: What is the final point of the parable of the youth and the king in 4:13-16?

options.text: Even a wise ruler who wins the crowd is soon forgotten, so applause is vapor.
options.note: The closing note falls on how quickly popularity fades.

options.text: Wisdom is better than status, yet its rewards do not last.
options.note: True, though the parable ends by stressing the fading of the crowd's favor.

options.text: It is better to be a poor wise youth than an old foolish king.
options.note: That is the opening line, but the parable's weight lands on fleeting applause.

options.text: Political success is the surest way to be remembered.
options.note: The parable teaches the opposite, that the successor is soon uncelebrated.

quiz.q: How does the ache of this chapter point toward Christ?

options.text: The oppressed with no comforter are answered by Christ and the Spirit, the Comforter God sends.
options.note: The missing comforter finds its answer in Jesus and the promised Spirit.

options.text: It shows a deep need for comfort that only God can meet.
options.note: True, and that comfort comes specifically through Christ and the Spirit.

options.text: It teaches that hard work will eventually be rewarded.
options.note: The chapter exposes striving as vapor and looks instead to God's comfort.

options.text: It has no connection to the gospel.
options.note: The New Testament answers its cry with the Comforter and the friend of sinners.

questions: The Teacher grieved that the oppressed had no comforter. Who around you is carrying tears with no one to comfort them, and how might God use you as part of His answer?
He names envy of the neighbor as the hidden engine of much striving. Where is comparison quietly driving your work, and what would it look like to lay it down?
For whom do I toil, asked the lonely man. Who are you working for, and is there anyone you are shutting out in the process?
Two are better than one, and a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. Where do you need to let someone lift you up rather than face things alone?
The crowd's favor faded within a generation. How does resting in God's unchanging love free you from chasing applause that never lasts?

translationNotes.note: Futile translates hevel, literally vapor or breath, the book's keyword; here envy driven striving is named as fleeting and ungraspable, not literally worthless.
Comforter renders a word for one who consoles; its repetition, and they had no comforter, drives home the aching absence the rest of Scripture answers in God the Comforter.
A cord of three strands is not quickly broken is a proverb of strength through union; it has long been applied to bonds that God Himself reinforces.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Ecclesiastes 4:1-16. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose within each verse.
